study_identification.author_journal_year: Floris et al., Nature Mental Health, 2024
study_identification.title: A multimodal neural signature of face processing in autism within the fusiform gyrus

study_characteristics.study_objective: To characterize the multimodal neural signature of face processing in autism within the fusiform gyrus (FFG), a core region of the face processing network, by combining normative modeling and linked independent component analysis across structural MRI, resting-state fMRI, task-fMRI, and EEG. The study aimed to elucidate how variation in brain anatomy and function jointly impacts face processing and social functioning in autism.

imaging_modality.answer: T1-weighted MRI; Resting-state fMRI (multi-echo EPI); Task-fMRI (Hariri face matching paradigm); EEG

preprocessing_pipeline.answer: CAT12/SPM12 for VBM structural preprocessing; FSL v5.0.6 for rs-fMRI preprocessing with ICA-AROMA for motion correction; SPM12 for task-fMRI preprocessing; Fieldtrip toolbox for EEG preprocessing; LCMV beamforming for EEG source analysis

quality_checking_detail.answer: Structural T1: CAT SPM pipeline quality ratings (0.5-10.5 scale), excluded images with excessive motion (N=37), clinically non-significant atypicalities (N=21), and failed preprocessing (N=3). Rs-fMRI: excluded scans with <180 volumes (N=8), meanFD>0.7mm (N=29), maxFD>7.6mm (N=38), low full-brain coverage (N=24), extreme values >4SD (N=12), failed preprocessing (N=1). Task-fMRI: excluded >20% of trials with meanFD>0.5mm (N=47). EEG: excluded technical/upload errors (N=33), incomplete battery (N=32), <20 artifact-free trials (N=9), <75% channels (N=2). Groups did not differ on quality metrics after exclusions.

site_effect_handling_detail.answer: Scanning site included as covariate in Bayesian Linear Regression normative models. Six acquisition sites: King's College London (GE MR750), Radboud University Nijmegen (Siemens Skyra), Cambridge (Siemens Verio), Utrecht (Philips 3T Achieva), Rome (GE Signa HDxTt), Mannheim (Siemens Trio). Site modeled along with age and sex in normative modeling framework.

response_variable.answer: Structural MRI: VBM-derived voxel-wise grey matter volumes within FFG; Rs-fMRI: seed-based connectivity between FFA and remaining FFG voxels (Fisher's z-transformed); Task-fMRI: T-contrast maps reflecting sensitivity to faces (faces vs. shapes condition); EEG: principal component of source-reconstructed activation across 18 cortical parcels per hemisphere within FFG

predictor_effects.answer: Age modeled with B-spline basis expansion for non-linear effects; Sex and scanning site as categorical covariates. All modeled as fixed effects in BLR framework.

nm_vldtn_handle_ns.reason: The study addresses some nuisance structure by including site, sex, and age in the normative model and applies extensive quality control for motion and image quality. Motion correction is particularly thorough (ICA-AROMA for rs-fMRI, framewise displacement exclusion criteria). However, the study does not explicitly discuss modeling heteroscedasticity (variance differences) or other complex nuisance structures beyond mean shifts. The B-spline age modeling addresses nonlinearity. Site is included as a covariate but no explicit harmonization method like ComBat is mentioned.
nm_vldtn_handle_ns.supporting_text: Normative models were derived in an unbiased manner across the entire sample under tenfold cross-validation. Here, we trained normative models using Bayesian linear regression for each brain imaging modality within the right and left FFG region of interest (ROI) independently using age, sex and scanning site as covariates. A B-spline basis expansion of the covariate vector was used to model nonlinear effects of age. ... ICA-AROMA has been demonstrated to remove head motion-related artifacts with high accuracy while preserving signal of interest.
nm_vldtn_handle_ns.location: Main paper: Methods section on Normative modeling (lines 193-194); Supplementary Methods: Normative Modeling section

nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.reason: The study uses 10-fold cross-validation to train and evaluate normative models on the same dataset (LEAP cohort). This is explicitly stated as a method to derive models in an unbiased manner. Cross-validation uses non-independent splits of the same training data.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.supporting_text: Normative models were derived in an unbiased manner across the entire sample under tenfold cross-validation. ... To estimate voxel-wise/time point-wise deviations for each modality in each individual, we derived normative probability maps that quantify the deviation from the normative model summarized in Z-scores. The accuracy of the normative model was evaluated using the correlation between the recorded and the predicted voxel values (Rho), the mean standardized log-loss, the explained variance and standardized mean squared error (Supplementary Fig. 1).

nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.reason: The study does not report validation on a held-out independent subset from the same domain (LEAP dataset). Only 10-fold cross-validation is used, which involves non-independent data splits. No separate test set from LEAP is mentioned.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.supporting_text: Normative models were derived in an unbiased manner across the entire sample under tenfold cross-validation.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.location: Main paper: Methods section, Normative modeling (line 194)

nm_vldtn_diff_domain.reason: The study does not validate the normative models on external datasets from different domains. All analyses are conducted within the LEAP cohort only.
nm_vldtn_diff_domain.supporting_text: No mention of external validation datasets in the methods or results sections.

clinical_dataset.answer: EU-AIMS/AIMS-2-TRIALS LEAP (autistic participants from the same cohort used for normative modeling)

deviation_metric.answer: Z-scores derived from normative probability maps; subject loadings on independent components (ICs) from LICA; extreme deviations defined as |Z|>2.6 (corresponding to 99.5th percentile)

clinical_application_and_analysis.association_analysis: Group comparison: Two-sample t-tests on IC subject loadings with FDR correction for multiple comparisons. Classification: Support Vector Machine (SVM) with linear kernel under 10-fold cross-validation comparing multimodal vs unimodal ICs (AUC as performance metric; permutation testing with 10,000 iterations for significance). Brain-behavior associations: Canonical Correlation Analysis (CCA) modeling multivariate relationship between multimodal ICs and clinical/cognitive features, with complete permutation inference (10,000 iterations), separately for social-communicative features vs non-social features. Controlled for age, sex, and site using Huh-Jhun residualization. Sensitivity analyses: tested robustness to handedness inclusion and restriction to right-handed individuals only.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_brief: Multimodal components driven by bilateral rs-fMRI, structure, right task-fMRI, and left EEG significantly differentiated autistic from non-autistic individuals and outperformed unimodal components; these components were specifically associated with social (but not non-social) functioning in autism.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_detailed: Among 50 independent components, one multimodal IC (IC44) showed significant group differences (t=3.5, pFDR=0.027) with autistic individuals having higher contributions. This component was driven by rs-fMRI R (48.5%), rs-fMRI L (35.0%), EEG L (11.6%), task-fMRI R (3.3%), and structure (1.5%). Spatially, IC44 implicated face-selective and retinotopic FFG regions differentially across hemispheres. Multimodal ICs (N=11) significantly outperformed unimodal ICs in autism classification (AUC multimodal=0.64 vs. unimodal=0.48, p<0.001). CCA revealed significant association between multimodal ICs and social-communicative features (r=0.65, pFDR=0.008) but not with non-social features (r=0.45, pFDR=0.64). The social association was primarily driven by IC37, IC38, IC44, and IC34 on the brain side, and by ADOS social affect, RMET, and Hariri face matching on the behavioral side. Functional modalities (especially rs-fMRI and EEG) contributed more than structural modalities. In the right hemisphere, higher-order face-selective regions showed both increased deviations (rs-fMRI connectivity and GM volume) and decreased deviations (task activation and FFA connectivity) in autism. Left hemisphere showed involvement of retinotopic and lower-order face-selective regions. Results were robust to handedness controls and multiple multimodality thresholds (85%-99%).
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_limitations: Limited to FFG region rather than whole-brain face processing network; relatively small sample size (N=204) for multimodal analysis given LEAP dataset size >600; insufficient female participants for sex-stratified analyses; small number of left-handed/ambidextrous participants limiting handedness analyses; task paradigm uses geometric shapes rather than face-like stimuli as comparison which may affect face specificity; combined upright and inverted faces in EEG analysis to preserve sample size; no external validation of findings in independent datasets; multimodal approaches require large samples with complete data across modalities which limits scalability.
clinical_application_and_analysis.application_notes: The study demonstrates that integrating multiple neuroimaging modalities through normative modeling and LICA provides superior sensitivity for detecting autism-related differences compared to unimodal approaches. The methodology combines two innovations: (1) normative modeling to derive individual-level deviations accounting for age/sex/site, and (2) LICA to optimally merge modalities with different feature numbers, spatial correlations, and units. Findings suggest functional modalities (concurrent neural activity) are more strongly tied to current social functioning than structural aspects, highlighting potential targets for interventions. The approach is particularly valuable for complex, heterogeneous conditions where multiple biological processes interact across spatial and temporal scales. Future work should explore whole-brain networks, sex differences with larger samples, and external validation across independent cohorts.

general_notes.general_notes: This study is notable for its sophisticated multimodal integration approach combining normative modeling with LICA in autism research. The LEAP dataset is a large European multicenter initiative (6 sites) with comprehensive clinical, cognitive, and multimodal neuroimaging assessment. The study demonstrates methodological rigor with extensive quality control, multiple sensitivity analyses, and consideration of confounds (handedness, site effects, motion). The normative modeling uses Z-score deviations rather than raw features, which prior work shows improves sensitivity. LICA optimally handles modalities with different characteristics through correction for effective degrees of freedom and automatic relevance determination priors. The focus on fusiform gyrus is justified by its role as core node in face processing network and fine-grained functional heterogeneity (face-selective FFA, body-selective, retinotopic regions). Clinical measures were comprehensively assessed and imputed using Extra Trees regression to handle missing data. The distinction between social-communicative vs non-social feature sets demonstrates specificity of findings. Medication use was tracked (30-50% of autistic participants on medications affecting nervous system - see Supplementary Table 11). Participants were predominantly Caucasian white (74.5%). The study used gold-standard diagnostic instruments (ADI-R, ADOS) with calibrated severity scores. Results showed differential hemispheric patterns: left hemisphere implicated retinotopic/lower-order regions (bottom-up processing), right hemisphere implicated higher-order face-selective regions (top-down processing), consistent with weak central coherence theory in autism. The temporal dimension of EEG provided complementary information to spatial MRI modalities. Model evaluation metrics (Rho, EV, MSLL, standardized MSE) were within recommended ranges. The study represents an important advancement in moving beyond univariate case-control comparisons to multivariate individual-level characterization in autism neuroimaging research.
